Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette: As a public defender, Julian had always been drawn to fighting for justice, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma he experienced while working with refugees. It was during this time that he witnessed the brutal suppression of a peaceful protest, and the memories of that day continued to haunt him. Julian's experiences had led him to believe that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place, where violence can erupt at any moment. This conviction had become all-consuming, driving him to be constantly on guard against potential threats. He would often find himself scanning his surroundings, searching for signs of danger, even in seemingly safe environments like his own home or office. His partner, Rachel, had noticed the change in him and tried to reassure him, but Julian couldn't shake off the feeling that he was just one misstep away from disaster. As a result of this hypervigilance, Julian began to monitor his thoughts obsessively, searching for any signs that he might be losing control or "going crazy." He would often catch himself thinking about the traumatic event and immediately try to push the memories away, fearing that if he dwelled on them too long, he would succumb to madness. This thought monitoring had become a habitual strategy for Julian, one that he employed whenever he felt threatened by his own emotions or thoughts. However, this avoidance behavior only seemed to exacerbate the problem. Whenever Julian's memories of the traumatic event surfaced, he would feel his body tense up, as if it was reliving the experience all over again. The visual images that haunted him were vivid and unshakeable – the sounds of gunfire, the screams of the protesters, the feeling of helplessness as he watched the chaos unfold. These bodily reenactments left Julian breathless and shaken, convinced that his body was trying to tell him something, but what? The memories also triggered a deep sense of emotional intensity, which would often leave Julian feeling overwhelmed and disoriented. He couldn't explain why these emotions felt so raw and unprocessed, even months after the event. The more he tried to suppress them, the more they seemed to seep into his daily life, affecting his relationships with Rachel and his colleagues. The sound of sirens or loud noises would startle Julian, making him jump in surprise. He became convinced that these sounds were a harbinger of danger, a warning sign that something was about to go terribly wrong. Even the silence seemed ominous to him, as if it was just a precursor to some unknown threat. His friends and family tried to reassure him, but Julian couldn't shake off the feeling that he was living in a state of constant threat. As time passed, Julian's avoidance behaviors became more pronounced. He stopped attending social gatherings or public events, fearing that they might trigger memories of the traumatic event. He also became increasingly withdrawn at work, struggling to connect with his clients or colleagues. His partner Rachel noticed the change and encouraged him to seek help, but Julian was hesitant, convinced that he could manage his symptoms on his own. However, as the months went by, Julian began to realize that his avoidance behaviors were not only affecting his relationships but also exacerbating his symptoms. He started to feel like he was trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance, with no clear escape route. It wasn't until he hit rock bottom – missing an important court hearing due to a panic attack triggered by a sudden noise – that Julian finally realized he needed help. With Rachel's support, Julian began to seek therapy, hoping to break free from the cycle of fear and avoidance that had consumed his life. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was determined to confront his demons head-on, rather than letting them dictate his every move. As he sat in the therapist's office, Julian felt a glimmer of hope – perhaps, just perhaps, he could learn to reclaim his life from the trauma that had haunted him for so long.
